claims.text: During rapid heating and cooling, formation of single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles is kinetically controlled by differential surface diffusion of the constituent metals.
Elements having lower surface energies and higher diffusivities preferentially segregate to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface segregation creates local composition fluctuations that drive phase separation and unstable or uncontrolled morphology.
Short diffusion times during rapid cooling cause surface segregation and transient compositional imbalance.
Preferential surface segregation produces core-shell-like elemental inhomogeneities.
A mild post-synthesis anneal permits sufficient atomic diffusion to rehomogenize local elemental fluctuations.
Annealing-driven rehomogenization occurs through entropy-driven mixing.
An intermediate annealing window exists in which rehomogenization can occur before extensive coarsening or secondary-phase growth.
Limited post-synthesis annealing stabilizes the desired single-phase solid solution.
Rapidly synthesized baseline nanoparticles tend to exhibit phase separation, surface segregation, and uncontrolled morphology.
Rapidly synthesized baseline nanoparticles have higher-than-expected apparent thermal decomposition temperatures.
The proposed anneal will reduce or eliminate elemental segregation and yield uniform elemental distributions throughout individual particles.
The proposed anneal will produce a more homogeneous single-phase crystal structure with fewer secondary phases.
The proposed anneal will improve control over particle morphology.
The proposed anneal will lower the effective thermal decomposition temperature relative to the rapid-quench baseline.
The mechanism applies to high-mixing-entropy, moderately size-mismatched, near-equiatomic noble-metal compositions such as combinations of Au, Ag, Pt, Pd, and Cu.
The mechanism may fail when elemental diffusivities or surface-energy differences are too disparate.
The mechanism may fail above the nanoscale because bulk diffusion becomes dominant.
Quantitative surface-diffusion coefficients and the critical annealing temperature-time product are unavailable for the proposed multielement noble-metal systems.

contradictions.description: The target is defined as containing more than five elements, but the concrete near-equiatomic example lists only Au, Ag, Pt, Pd, and Cu, which is exactly five elements.

The anneal is said to stabilize the single-phase structure, yet it is also predicted to lower its effective decomposition temperature. Without a distinct definition of 'decomposition temperature,' lower decomposition temperature is in tension with increased structural stability.
